note: Editorial layer for the article set. Every factual statement in every article below is either (a) a value already published in data/products.json, which carries its own source id, or (b) a direct quote from an Amazon Associates, FTC or eCFR document already registered in data/sources.json. No claim of first-hand testing appears anywhere, no superlative is asserted as fact, and no Amazon price, star rating or review count is used. Articles that would need a hands-on measurement are deliberately not written.
discipline: A factual sentence must carry a citation to a registered source. A sentence that states a view, a decision rule or a judgement is marked as such by the rendering (the 'How to read this' box) and is never presented as a verified fact. Where an official source is silent, the article says it is silent instead of filling the gap.

articles.title: Dual-basket or countertop oven? The 8-quart question nobody answers
articles.standfirst: Two 3-quart drawers and one 26-quart cavity solve opposite problems. Here is the documented difference, and the one measurement that decides it for your kitchen.
articles.target_query: dual basket vs air fryer oven

sections.h: The two machines are not competing for the same job
paras: A dual-basket air fryer is one appliance pretending to be two. The Chefman 6 Qt splits a {{6 Qt / 5.67 L}} cavity into {{Two 3-quart baskets}} and gives each its own time and temperature, then adds Sync Finish so the shorter cook is delayed to land with the longer one.

A countertop oven is a different shape of compromise: one big cavity, many modes. The Emeril 26 QT is documented at {{26 qt / 24.6 L (manual: 1,519 cu in)}} with a dual-speed fan, a rotisserie, and French doors.

sections.h: What you can actually cook, stated in the manufacturer's own numbers
paras: The dual-basket unit's ceiling is {{450 °F / 235 °C, held for 2 minutes, for extra browning}}, over a {{200–450 °F / 95–235 °C}} range.

The oven's documented range is {{75–500 °F / 25–260 °C}} on {{120 V / 60 Hz}} at a rated {{1700 W}}. It is the only unit here that goes below 200 °F, which is what makes proofing and dehydrating possible rather than nominal.
What neither page states is how evenly either one cooks. That number does not exist on a manufacturer page, and this site does not invent it.

sections.h: The measurement that decides it
paras: Footprint, not capacity. The dual-basket unit is {{13.38 × 11.81 × 10.63 in / 33.98 × 30 × 27 cm}} and weighs {{13.3 lb / 6.03 kg}}. The oven is {{16.9 D × 15.8 W × 14.8 H in}}.
Put a tape measure on the counter and add the clearance the manual asks for behind and above the unit. A 26-quart oven that does not fit under your cabinets is not a 26-quart oven; it is a return.

sections.h: The honest summary
paras: Buy the dual-basket if you cook two things at two temperatures and want them to finish together. Buy the oven if you want one cavity that can also toast, proof and rotisserie, and you have measured the space.

If you want a single large basket instead, the third product in this set is documented as {{8 qt (brand also sells a 5 qt version of the same product page)}} and {{Designed for 4–6 people}} — but read that product's own page before you buy, because its Amazon listing and its brand page disagree about the temperature ceiling.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. Every number above is quoted from the manufacturer's own product page or owner's manual and is linked in the source column.

articles.title: What "450 °F" actually means on an air fryer listing
articles.standfirst: On one Chefman model it is a two-minute finishing blast. On another it is a setting the manual never mentions. The badge is the same. The feature is not.

sections.h: Three different things get called "450 °F"
paras: **A full-cycle ceiling.** The Chefman 6 Qt documents a {{200–450 °F / 95–235 °C}} working range, with Hi-Fry documented as {{450 °F / 235 °C, held for 2 minutes, for extra browning}}.

**A finishing blast on a lower-ceiling unit.** Chefman's 8 Qt High Fry model is a different SKU from the stainless one this site maps: it publishes a Hi-Fry temperature of 450 °F / 232 °C and a four-function list alongside it, so the two are documented as separate things on the same page. See flag F33.

**A marketing claim with no matching manual page.** This is the case the site flags rather than resolves: the Amazon listing for the stainless 8-quart unit advertises a 450 °F Hi-Fry option, but the brand page for the model the site maps to that listing documents a {{200–400 °F}} range and four food presets.

sections.h: Why the badge matters commercially
paras: A higher ceiling is the difference between browning and steaming. But a "450 °F" badge can mean a full-cycle setting, a two-minute finish mode, or a number a copywriter typed. The only way to tell is the manual that ships with the unit — and for a listing whose model is not stated, that manual is the only document that is definitely about your machine.

sections.h: What this site does about it, and what it refuses to do
paras: It publishes both claims, side by side, with a link to each, and asserts neither. It also publishes the fact that a second Chefman 8-quart SKU exists whose documented Hi-Fry and function list match the Amazon title exactly — which makes "one of these pages is stale" the less likely explanation and "these are two different units" the more likely one.
It does not pick a winner. A fabricated resolution would be worse than a visible conflict, because you would buy on the strength of it.

sections.h: How to check in thirty seconds
paras: Open the listing. Find the model number in the product-information block. Search that exact model on the manufacturer's site. Read the specification block on that page, not the bullet points in the carousel. If the model number is absent — which it is on all three listings in this set — you are relying on the brand's word about a unit you cannot identify, and you should say so to yourself before you check out.

articles.closing_note: This explainer states no temperature for the ASIN behind product 3, because no official source states it unambiguously. That gap is published on the Flagged for review page.

articles.title: 25 presets, 24 presets, or 10-in-1? One brand page says all three
articles.standfirst: A single official product page contradicts itself four ways. That is not a scandal; it is what an unmaintained product page looks like. Here is how to read it.
articles.target_query: emeril french door air fryer 360 how many presets

sections.h: The four numbers, all from official sources
paras: On 2026-11-14 the Emeril Everyday product page for the 26 QT French Door AirFryer carried **25 Cooking Pre-sets** in its specification block, **24 one-touch cooking presets** in its description paragraph, and a feature heading reading **10-In-1 Versatility**. One of its carousel images is a file named `11-in-1_convection_oven_in_action.png`. Amazon's listing title for the same product says **24 cooking functions**.
Five official statements, four different numbers, one product.

sections.h: The manual is the tiebreaker a shopper can actually use
paras: The owner's manual linked from that same page names 24 presets for model FAFO-001, listed one by one: Airfry, Fries, Bacon, Grill, Eggs, Fish, Ribs, Defrost, Steak, Vegetables, Wings, Bake, Rotisserie, Toast, Chicken, Pizza, Pastry, Proof, Broil, Slow Cook, Roast, Dehydrate, Reheat, Warm.
That is a countable list on the document that ships with the unit, and it agrees with the description text and with Amazon. It does not agree with the page's own specification block.

sections.h: What this means for a buyer
paras: Nothing about the appliance changes when a marketing page is wrong. What changes is how much of the page you should trust. A page with four different preset counts, placeholder copy in its help section, and a carousel asset named for a feature its own heading contradicts is a page that was assembled quickly and not re-read.

The specifications that are singular and specific on that page — the dimensions, the 24.6-litre capacity and the 120-volt rating stated in that same block — are the ones to plan around, because a copy-paste error is less likely to survive in a field a shipping department needs.

sections.h: Why the site still shows no preset count for this product
paras: Because two official sources agreeing is not the same as the manufacturer publishing one number. The owner's manual names 24, so the specification row is published against the manual and not against the marketing page — and the conflict is published on the Flagged for review page so you can see exactly what was reconciled and what was not.

articles.closing_note: The manual's 24-preset list is countable and is cited to the manual. The 25, 24, 10-in-1 and 11-in-1 statements are all published verbatim on the brand's own page and are recorded on the Flagged for review page rather than smoothed over.

articles.kicker: Why this site looks like this
articles.title: Why this affiliate site shows no Amazon prices, ratings or review counts
articles.standfirst: It is not an oversight and it is not humility. Amazon's Program Policies only permit those numbers under two specific conditions, and this site meets neither.
articles.target_query: why affiliate site no amazon price

sections.h: The rule, quoted
paras: From the Associates Program Participation Requirements, section 2(b): prices and availability may be shown only if "**(a) we serve the link in which that price and availability data are displayed, or (b) you obtain Product pricing and availability data via Creators API or PA API**" and comply with the License requirements.
And from section 6(t): you may not display customer reviews or star ratings "**unless you have obtained a link to that customer review or star rating through Creators API or PA API**".

This site is a static set of pages generated from a JSON file. Amazon does not serve its links here, and there are no Creators or PA-API credentials behind it. Both conditions fail, so both categories of data are absent.

sections.h: The second rule people miss: no price tracking
paras: Section 6(y) is blunt: "**Unless otherwise agreed by Amazon, your Site must not have price tracking and/or price alerting functionality.**"

That rules out the most common affiliate feature of all — a price-history chart, a "price drop" alert, a "lowest ever" badge. A site that shows a price it scraped yesterday is not just out of date; it is the thing the clause is aimed at.

sections.h: What a compliant site can honestly show instead
paras: Manufacturer list prices, clearly labelled as the brand's own list price rather than a retailer price. Physical specifications, because the manufacturer owns those facts and they do not change by the hour. Commission rates from Amazon's own published table. And the gaps, named.
A number that is missing on purpose is a different object from a number that is missing by neglect. The first one a reader can trust the rest of the page around.

sections.h: The disclosure that does appear on every page
paras: Operating Agreement section 5 requires the Associate to "**clearly and prominently state**" the identification "**As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.**" — that sentence sits in the bar at the top of every page in this build, and the build fails if it is missing from any page.

The FTC's rule is the other half. A material connection must be disclosed "**clearly and conspicuously**" (16 CFR §255.5(a)), and the FTC's own guidance says the disclosure has to be placed with the endorsement rather than on a separate about page. Hence the persistent bar rather than a link in the footer.

articles.closing_note: Every quotation in this article is from a page linked in its source column and was read live. Nothing in it is legal advice; it is the rule text plus how this build implements it.

articles.title: Two 3-quart drawers or one 8-quart basket: which actually feeds four people?
articles.standfirst: The total volume is nearly identical. The cooking is not, and the difference is what you do when the first batch finishes.
articles.target_query: dual basket vs single basket air fryer

sections.h: The arithmetic, from the manufacturer's own pages
paras: The dual-basket unit is {{6 Qt / 5.67 L}} as {{Two 3-quart baskets}}. The single-basket unit is {{8 qt (brand also sells a 5 qt version of the same product page)}}, documented as {{Designed for 4–6 people}}.
So the single basket holds more at once — a third more — and the two drawers hold less per drawer but can run independently. That is the whole trade, and everything else is detail.

sections.h: What Sync Finish is actually for
paras: {{Sync Finish}} delays the start of the shorter cook so both baskets finish together; a separate Sync Baskets function copies time and temperature to the second basket.

This matters because the failure mode of batch cooking is the second batch going cold while the first one waits. A machine that plans both drawers to land at the same moment solves a problem that a bigger single basket creates rather than solves.

sections.h: Where the single basket wins
paras: One big batch of one thing. A whole chicken, a full tray of fries, a pile of wings for a crowd. Splitting 8 quarts into two 3-quart drawers means every basket-shaped item has to fit a 3-quart drawer.

The documented one-touch presets on the single-basket unit are {{Fries, Chicken, Fish, Meat (one-touch)}}, and the manual publishes a default for each: {{Default 400 °F / 15 min · Meat 375 °F / 18 min · Chicken 375 °F / 22 min · Fish 350 °F / 10 min · Fries 400 °F / 20 min}}.

sections.h: The decision, stated as a decision
paras: If most of your meals are two components that should finish together, the dual basket is the better tool and the capacity number is a red herring. If most of your meals are one component in quantity, the 8-quart is the better tool and the Sync Finish feature is a feature you would never press.
This is a judgement about how people cook, not a fact from a manufacturer page, and it is labelled as such.

articles.closing_note: Neither unit was tested. Capacity, presets, defaults and features are quoted from the brand's product pages and the owner's manual for the single-basket model.
